title: STUDENT VOICE: I turned down my dream college for a far more affordable state school. It still hurts
summary:
I fell in love with Tufts University as soon as I stepped on the campus right outside of Boston. I knew that financial aid was a huge concern, but I decided to take the chance and apply, hoping that the finances would work themselves out.  On the day decisions were due, I refreshed my inbox […]

The post STUDENT VOICE: I turned down my dream college for a far more affordable state school. It still hurts appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
I fell in love with Tufts University as soon as I stepped on the campus right outside of Boston. I knew that financial aid was a huge concern, but I decided to take the chance and apply, hoping that the finances would work themselves out.

On the day decisions were due, I refreshed my inbox on my phone all day, nerves building as the hours went by. Finally, at 7 p.m., I saw the email I’d been waiting for. After a deep breath, I opened the link.

I started screaming. I got in! But it was not to be.

For many students, getting accepted to their dream school is the finish line. For me, it was only another race, figuring out whether I could actually afford to attend. The full cost to my family would approach $100,000 annually, including housing and food plans.

The university’s website notes that Tufts meets 100 percent of all demonstrated need, so I was hopeful. Yet my financial aid notification, which arrived a few weeks after the acceptance, stated that I did not qualify for need-based assistance and would have to pay close to the full amount. My heart sank.

My story is not unique. The college application process puts many families in limbo when they are not wealthy enough to comfortably pay full tuition, but also do not qualify for sufficient financial aid. A recent poll said just 12 percent of Americans believe four-year colleges are affordable.

My parents are both not-for-profit professionals with graduate degrees. Along with their full-time jobs, they both work additional jobs. The funds they have saved through investments like New York’s 529 state-sponsored savings plans to cover my undergraduate education (along with my two younger brothers’) are nowhere near the amounts that Tufts expects us to contribute.

In September, 2025, Tufts announced that U.S. students whose families earn less than $150,000 a year are eligible for grants that cover the full cost of tuition, beginning this fall. This might sound promising, but it won’t help all the families who make more but still can’t afford the full cost without substantial aid or loans.

The school’s website does have information on different kinds of aid, along with a financial aid calculator for prospective students. When my family filled it out, the calculator said we could expect aid that would lower the net price of tuition to around $60,000 or so, making Tufts a possible option.

After I got in, my parents and I formally requested a reevaluation of my financial aid award. A number of calls and emails followed. The final package Tufts offered included a $3,500 loan and an estimated $2,500 in potential earnings from work-study wages, if I took a job on campus.

I would still be responsible for coming up with $94,536 dollars a year.

(Editor’s note: Officials in the financial aid office at Tufts University said that while it cannot comment on aid offered to individual students, its net price calculator is designed to give families a reasonable estimate of their potential financial aid eligibility, based on the information they provide. After a prospective student applies for aid, Tufts also reviews information reported on the FAFSA and CSS Profile, along with required supporting documentation. If the information provided through the calculator differs from what is ultimately verified through the formal financial aid process, the student’s financial aid eligibility and award may change accordingly.)

Attending my dream school would leave me with about $270,000 debt (I calculated this by the using the amount Tufts said I would have to pay minus what a state school would charge to get the amount I would have to borrow over the course of four years). That was not an option. I will likely need loans for law or graduate school, and I do not want to begin adulthood carrying overwhelming undergraduate debt.

Fortunately, I had been accepted by several other universities. After comparing finances, I will enroll at Binghamton University in New York next fall, after a gap year studying in Israel. As a resident of New York state, I will have annual estimated costs of roughly $32,000 a year, less than a third of the cost of Tufts.

Related: If higher education wants to rebuilt public trust, start by making college affordable

My parents and I decided together that this school would be the best fit for me for several reasons, but finances specifically. My parents strongly believe that it is not worth putting myself into debt for an undergraduate degree.

Giving up Tufts meant missing out on an elite school with a more competitive reputation and global connections, but I know that I will be successful at Binghamton. I plan to study political science, and hope to graduate with a degree and career opportunities, debt-free.

I am excited about my future at Binghamton, and I know I will receive an excellent education. However, I should not have had to choose between my dream school and my financial future. No student should.

If we truly believe that higher education is a pathway to opportunity, then affordability cannot be treated as an afterthought. Students should be able to choose colleges based on where they will learn, grow and succeed — not simply on which option will leave them with the least debt.

Shir Levenson plans to enroll at SUNY Binghamton in New York in the fall of 2027.

This story about college costs was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education. Sign up for Hechinger’s weekly newsletter.

title: What Are We Missing About Student Mental Health?
summary:
What Are We Missing About Student Mental Health? Joshua.Bay Thu, 10/08/2026 - 03:00 AM Harvard’s Alexis Redding discusses how the entire college experience shapes student well-being and what it takes to build a culture of care. Byline(s) Joshua Bay What Are We Missing About Student Mental Health?
Joshua.Bay Thu, 10/08/2026 - 03:00 AM

Harvard’s Alexis Redding discusses how the entire college experience shapes student well-being and what it takes to build a culture of care.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Colleges have devoted growing attention and resources to student well-being in recent years, but supporting mental health goes far beyond what happens inside a counseling center.

Students’ well-being can be shaped by nearly every part of the college experience—from the expectations they bring with them to campus and the academic, financial and social pressures they encounter to how they navigate setbacks, uncertainty and the transition into adulthood.

Alexis Redding, a developmental psychologist and professor at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, joined Inside Higher Ed student success reporter Joshua Bay on Voices of Student Success to talk about what colleges may still misunderstand about student mental health, how the broader college experience impacts students’ well-being, where normal stress and struggle fit into the conversation, and what it would look like for institutions to build a culture of care that supports students throughout college and beyond.

Follow us on Apple Podcasts and Spotify

Here are five key takeaways from Redding on what it takes to support student well-being across the college experience.

Student mental health is shaped by the entire college experience.

Redding said higher education often thinks too narrowly about student mental health by focusing primarily on the years students are enrolled in college. Instead, she said, institutions should consider the experiences that affect students’ well-being before they arrive on campus and as they prepare to leave.

That includes the pressures students experience during the college admissions process as well as the expectations they bring with them about what college should look like academically, socially and personally.

Redding noted that in her book Mental Health in College, she also explores for students “the transition into the workforce or into graduate school and making those decisions, because it is yet another moment of transition that really feeds into what happens during the college years.”

She added that the pressure to have a successful or even transformative college experience can affect students’ mental health when reality doesn’t match those expectations.

“The story of college that we tell culturally on Instagram, in movies, in our retelling is that college will be the best four years of your life,” Redding said. “For a lot of people, college is not four years. It is longer or shorter than that. But more importantly, you’ll have great moments in college, but you will also have challenging moments because you are in transition.”

“What’s really important for us to do is to start to tell a much more honest story about college,” she added. “Every student has their own version of feeling lonely and unsettled, and almost no student shares it with each other. They all think that they are struggling alone [and] that they are uniquely doing something wrong.”

Not every struggle is a mental health crisis.

Redding said it’s important to distinguish between students who are in need of clinical care and should be referred to a counseling center and those who are experiencing more common struggles associated with college and emerging adulthood.

“The vast majority of students are struggling in more typical ways,” Redding said. “Developmental issues of being in a moment of transition, doing something hard for the first time, being disconnected from home or navigating multiple responsibilities at once.”

She said it’s important for higher education leaders to be able to discern between the two so “we don’t overreact to the student who’s having a typical bad day, and we don’t underreact to the student who has a clinical concern.”

Redding emphasized that the instinct to refer students to clinical care comes from a good place, but she said treating every expression of struggle as a mental health crisis can prevent students from receiving the kind of support they were actually seeking.

“We are so worried about missing somebody who has a clinical need, and that is the right instinct,” Redding said. “The issue with leading with that instinct is that we tend to overreact when a student is having the typical bad day.”

Redding noted that when students approach faculty about a bad grade, issues with financial aid, struggles with a roommate or difficulties with their commute, immediately referring them to the counseling center because they say they’re struggling can “[shut] down the lines of communication with the caring campus adult who they sought out to have a conversation with and [escalate] it.”

There is no single student mental health experience.

Redding noted that today’s college students include community college students, adult learners, veterans, student parents, first-generation students and many others whose lives may look very different from the traditional image of an 18-year-old living on campus. Those differences, she said, should shape how institutions approach student well-being rather than designing around a one-size-fits-all student experience.

“When we design programs and policies and practices thinking that everybody is in residence, is attending full-time, we set up friction points in the campus or in the institution that don’t need to exist,” Redding said.

She said institutions can identify those friction points in a range of ways, from creating focus groups with students to putting themselves in the position of the different students they serve and examining how easy—or difficult—it is to access the resources they need.

If a commuter student is “trying to get help at the dean of students’ office, trying to go hang out in the queer students’ office and build community there, or trying to get counseling when it is offline when they arrive on campus, that sends a particular signal that ‘they don’t understand my experience here.’”

“Beginning to think through all of those ways of experiencing campus can empower you to fix that,” Redding said. “To not put things behind a paywall that a prospective student might actually need to know about, like the hours of the childcare center or how much it costs.”

Awareness alone won’t solve the student mental health challenge.

With World Mental Health Day coming up on Oct. 10, Redding noted that colleges increasingly use moments like it to raise awareness and encourage students to seek help. But she said the next phase of this work should include not only addressing clinical concerns but also helping students understand and navigate common experiences such as loneliness, disconnection and the emotional ups and downs of college.

“What I would love to make sure we’re doing simultaneously with moving forward on all of the powerful work we have done to destigmatize the conversation around mental health is to continue to uplift this conversation about the typical bad days and what students should expect,” Redding said.

In conversations with higher education leaders, Redding often points to the W curve, a model illustrating the typical pattern of emotional highs and lows students may experience as they adjust to college. Understanding when those dips tend to occur, she said, can help institutions think more intentionally about when students may need additional connection and support.

“We know that so many colleges and universities put all of their programming, especially for first-year students, during orientation week, and the enthusiasm and excitement of building community and the programming starts to drop off,” Redding said. “Having these midpoints of the semester and reupping that kind of enthusiasm and programming at the beginning of the second semester actually meets where students are on the W curve at the moments where they have these profound dips.”

Supporting student well-being takes the whole institution.

Redding said building a culture of care requires institutions to consider how students experience support not only through formal mental health services but also in their classrooms, advising relationships and everyday interactions on campus.

One example she has seen is faculty creating “warm” policies in their syllabi that signal to students that they care about them as people. That can include explaining how to request an extension or ask for help and sharing information about resources such as food pantries and other basic needs supports.

“We tend to underestimate how important it is for students to have those moments to ask a really basic question,” Redding said. “Let them ask the really basic question, because it’s almost always a preamble to the much harder question that’s two questions down the line.

“Creating the spaces where they can do that and they can see that you really care, that you are doing this work because you want them to succeed, makes a big difference,” she added.

For Redding, creating that kind of environment also requires thinking more broadly about what student success ultimately means. Rather than focus only on whether students persist and earn a degree, she said colleges should give students opportunities to explore who they are and what they want from their lives beyond graduation.

“We want to be preparing our students for a life that is meaningful to them, and that means that we have to carve out the space while they are with us for them to do genuine exploration and to make big decisions with scaffolding,” Redding said. “A college experience that, to me, is successful is one where every student can ask and answer those questions for themselves, and we can create the space where that happens.”

title: Trump Proposes $70K Fee for Foreign Student Work Program
summary:
Trump Proposes $70K Fee for Foreign Student Work Program Johanna Alonso Thu, 10/08/2026 - 03:00 AM The Department of Homeland Security argues in the proposal that any negative impacts on employers or institutions are outweighed by its goal of reducing fraud. Byline(s) Johanna Alonso Trump Proposes $70K Fee for Foreign Student Work Program
Johanna Alonso Thu, 10/08/2026 - 03:00 AM

The Department of Homeland Security argues in the proposal that any negative impacts on employers or institutions are outweighed by its goal of reducing fraud.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
The Trump administration wants to charge a significant fee for international students to work temporarily in the U.S. after graduation—a proposal that some warned would further deter foreigners from studying in the United States.

Any F-1 student looking to start optional practical training, the program that allows international students to work in the U.S., would be subject to a $70,000 fee, while STEM OPT extensions would cost $30,000. Institutions would be expected to pay the fee when they “recommend an F-1 nonimmigrant student for any type of OPT,” according to the proposal released Wednesday.

Officials wrote that the goal of the fee is to curb cases of OPT fraud, in which students use OPT to remain in the country but are not actually doing legitimate work; the Department of Homeland Security cites a local NBC investigation that found over 4,000 had used shell companies to falsify employment records to receive OPT. It also cited a recent DHS investigation that it said found 10,000 F-1 students on OPT who “were working for highly suspect employers.”

DHS hopes the fee will encourage colleges to recommend “only high achieving eligible F-1 nonimmigrant students who are pursuing OPT directly related to [the students’] major program of study, thereby ensuring both F-1 nonimmigrant students and employers benefit from OPT.”

The rule is not yet final. The public has 30 days to comment on the rule before it is finalized. DHS will then have to review and respond to the comments before issuing a final rule. Students approved for OPT before the fee takes effect won’t have to pay it.

Nearly 290,000 students were authorized for OPT or STEM OPT in 2024, at which point the number of students participating in OPT had been steadily increasing for several years. DHS expects the fee to lead to a smaller pool of participants.

The fee has been a long time coming. Conservative leaders have long criticized OPT for the fraud issues presented in the proposed rule, but also for, in their view, taking job opportunities away from American citizens. Recently, several Republican legislators have called to end OPT.

And the administration has already used fees to dissuade other nonimmigrants from working in the U.S. The administration has twice attempted to attach a $100,000 fee to H-1B visas, which allow companies to hire skilled foreign workers and which are frequently used by institutions of higher education and medical centers; the first iteration was tossed out because the judge ruled DHS needed approval from Congress to implement the fee.

Reports first emerged in November that the administration was working on a plan to end or limit the program, and international education leaders have warned the other new policies could negatively affect OPT.

On Wednesday, international educators expressed concern about the proposed fee, arguing that the rule will further drive international students away from U.S. universities and from jobs in high-demand fields.

“OPT enables international students to gain the same hands-on experience as their domestic peers while filling labor shortages in high-demand STEM fields and generating jobs for U.S. workers on U.S. soil,” wrote Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators. “Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership.”

Aw also cited research from the Niskanen Center in 2023 and the National Foundation for American Policy that both found that OPT does not take away job opportunities from U.S. workers. NAFSA’s own research has indicated that international students and their families contribute tens of billions of dollars to the U.S. economy annually.

OPT is also a major draw for international students to the U.S., meaning that the loss of the opportunity could result in a further decline in international student enrollment, which has already affected some U.S. universities that rely on tuition revenue from that population.

But DHS argues in the rule that the impact on institutions is not significant enough to outweigh the national security concerns, writing that colleges “should be able to attract foreign students without relying on OPT and STEM OPT, as students rely on myriad factors when applying for and selecting a school to pursue a course of study.”

The rule, too, says that employers should not be adversely impacted: “To the extent employers [sic] staffing levels may be impacted by this proposed fee, they can minimize this impact by recruiting U.S. citizens or candidates with other lawful work authorization to fill the vacancies.”

In a statement, the Association of Public and Land-grant Universities expressed doubts that colleges and universities can afford to shoulder the $70,000 fee, calling the proposal “deeply flawed.”

The OPT rule notes that institutions may pass the fee off to student, to the employer or to the student body at large, if they wish.

title: Fighting Back on Restrictions to Internships for International Students
summary:
Fighting Back on Restrictions to Internships for International Students Johanna Alonso Thu, 10/08/2026 - 03:00 AM The federal government attempted to quietly change the requirements for a long-standing policy allowing international students to participate in internships. Four higher ed groups say the method they used was illegal. Byline(s) Johanna Alonso Fighting Back on Restrictions to Internships for International Students
Johanna Alonso Thu, 10/08/2026 - 03:00 AM

The federal government attempted to quietly change the requirements for a long-standing policy allowing international students to participate in internships. Four higher ed groups say the method they used was illegal.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
In August, international services professionals at colleges across the country received an unwelcome surprise: The Student and Exchange Visitor Program, an office within the Department of Homeland Security, sent what it called a “reminder of liability” about curricular practical training, or CPT, the program that allows international students to partake in internships.

But according to a lawsuit filed this week by four higher education associations, that notice did not contain a simple reminder—it fundamentally changed the rules regarding how international students can partake in CPT. The program was established in 1947, and regulations clarified in 1964 that international students could complete an internship if it was “directly related” to their major and was “an integral part of an established curriculum.” Since then, international students have been allowed to complete any for-credit internships, and they could complete noncredit internships if they were mandatory for degree completion.

The August memo, however, said that international students could only participate in CPT if the internship was required for graduation—regardless of whether it is for credit. If that rule was broken, institutions could lose their ability to enroll international students, and the staff members who authorize CPT could be held criminally liable. A subsequent Aug. 24 message reiterated those standards.

Led by the Association of American Universities, the organizations say those memos were not the right venue for changing regulations about how the program works, even if DHS characterized that change as a clarification.

The messages caused immediate panic among international students, who reported via social media and the site CPT Map, which uses student-reported data to show which institutions have stopped approving CPT, that their institutions had either paused processing or had officially rejected their applications for fall internships.

“This is so upsetting because I paid for the internship class to do my CPT (1.5k almost) and if they keep it on pause rather than deciding, I can’t get a refund either,” one Reddit user posted on the University of North Texas’s subreddit. “I’ve lost my TA position as well that would’ve helped with my tuition.”

In another post, a student who said they attend Texas A&M University wrote that they were worried about the authorization for their for-credit internship being rejected after the add/drop deadline, leaving them unable to maintain their status; undergraduate international students are required to take at least 12 credit hours each semester.

The change comes amid a slew of actions by the Trump administration that advocates say negatively impact international students, including creating a rule to limit how long international students may study in the U.S. without getting an extension. With the CPT memo and a newly proposed rule placing a significant fee on optional practical training, which allows students to work in the U.S. after finishing their degree, the administration has zeroed in on the ability of international students to work in the U.S.

Conservative politicians have traditionally opposed OPT in particular, claiming that it takes opportunities from American workers and opens the door for visa fraud. CPT has been less controversial, though Day-1 CPT—university programs where students work while they study from their first day of school—have also faced scrutiny and sometimes been characterized as schemes that allow students to pay tuition to work in the U.S.

But institutions and international education experts argue that examples of misuse are few and far between. Internships, meanwhile, are an invaluable and unique element of the U.S. higher education system, and taking away the opportunity to complete them from international students puts those students at a significant disadvantage in the job market. Plus, OPT and CPT are among the biggest draws for international students to study in the U.S., and this policy shift could lead already-dwindling international student numbers to worsen still.

In the wake of the memo, at least 130 institutions have paused or restricted CPT authorization, according to the CPT Map, though the true number is likely higher due to the crowdsourced nature of the site.

It’s unclear how many students would be impacted by the policy shift if it remains in place, though the lawsuit states that over 130,000 students participated in CPT in 2024. Although a small number of institutions require at least one internship to graduate, others would have to limit CPT to just a handful of majors that require internships to graduate. On a web page regarding CPT, the University of Colorado at Boulder lists 18 majors, mostly in education, the arts and engineering, that will qualify, out of its 238 degree programs. The University of California, Irvine, lists 17 eligible programs out of 216 total and notes that some master’s and doctoral dissertations may qualify.

In the lawsuit, the organizations argue that the government’s insistence that CPT must be required for a student to graduate is not a clarification of an existing rule. Rather, they say, it is a change to a more than 60-year-old regulation and guidance from a memo can’t supersede formal regulations under the Administrative Procedure Act, which governs how federal agencies make regulations.

If the Student and Exchange Visitor Program wanted to change how CPT works, the plaintiffs argue, it should have done so through a proper regulatory process, including a notice-and-comment period—not via memos to institutions, known as broadcast messages.

“The Broadcasts mark a sudden, unexplained reversal from the federal government’s prior longstanding position that training opportunities for which students receive academic credit are eligible for CPT, even if they are not mandatory for everyone to obtain the degree,” the complaint reads.

The plaintiffs also argue that the memos are written in a way that applies the new CPT requirements retroactively, thus opening institutions and employees up to penalties for past authorizations.

The lawsuit asks the judge to toss out the new requirements for CPT.

“The Broadcasts are already inflicting serious and mounting harm,” the complaint reads. “Students have borne the most immediate blow: institutions have been forced to halt CPT authorizations midstream, cancelling long-planned internships and other placements—including opportunities scheduled for this academic year that students secured months ago and, in many cases, cannot replace. For students nearing the end of their programs, these opportunities are lost forever; for others, the training that their degree programs were designed around is now out of reach.”

title: Vancouver’s language school sector faces a new reality
summary:
EC English and ILAC's shock closures last month lay bare the challenges that have blighted Vancouver's language school sector for years, writes Patricio Alfaro.

The post Vancouver’s language school sector faces a new reality appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
For generations of international students, studying English in Vancouver has been a personal goal: improving their language skills, experiencing Canada and, for many, preparing for further education, employment or immigration.

That goal has been shaken this month by the sudden closure of two of the best-known brands in the international language school industry. As widely reported, EC English announced on September 14 the immediate closure of all 25 of its schools worldwide, including its Vancouver and Toronto operations.

Four days later, the International Language Academy of Canada (ILAC) announced that it had filed for bankruptcy protection and immediately ceased operations.

Industry commentary following the closures suggests the Canadian education market is restructuring, not only for language schools, but also for career programs.

The high-volume private English school may give way to public institutions with in-house language centres that are positioned to reclaim market share.

Smaller schools may also be well positioned to serve some of the demand left behind: independent schools that never scaled up to expensive commercial real estate footprints, or that offer online programs.

A sudden shock for students

The issue is more than the disappearance of a school name. The closures left students uncertain about what would happen to their tuition payments and how they could continue their studies.

The British Columbia government’s Private Training Institutions Branch confirmed that ILAC Education Group and several related institutions surrendered their provincial designation certificates effective September 18. Eligible students may claim compensation from the provincial Student Tuition Protection Fund.

To help students finish their studies, Languages Canada is arranging placements in similar programs.

For Vancouver, that raises a larger question: what does international English education look like when the assumptions that supported the industry for years are no longer holding

But replacing a school is not always as simple as finding another classroom. It can also mean a financial loss: students usually arrange accommodation, flights, insurance, and other services well in advance of their studies, and those costs may not be recoverable.

Why is this happening now?

The closures come after several years of major changes to Canada’s international student system that extend beyond language schools.

Federal restrictions on international student numbers, changes to study permits, and other regulatory measures have significantly altered the market on which private education institutions operate. All of this is pushing institutions across the international education sector to adjust to a smaller and more regulated market.

For Vancouver, that raises a larger question: what does international English education look like when the assumptions that supported the industry for years are no longer holding?

A smaller market will require different models

The collapse of large operators also draws attention to another part of Vancouver’s language sector: smaller, specialised schools that are adopting different approaches.

For students whose main objective is to achieve a particular English-language test score, individualised instruction and preparation focused on a specific examination may be more relevant than a large campus-based program. Online, exam-focused instruction for tests such as IELTS or CELPIP makes it possible to begin studying without first travelling to Canada.

The difference between campus-based and individualised instruction may become increasingly important. For many years, the language-school industry was built around the campus experience. Students travelled to Canada, attended classes in groups, lived with host families or in student accommodation, and spent weeks or months immersed in Vancouver life.

That model is not disappearing. But the recent closures demonstrate how exposed large, campus-dependent organisations can become when international enrolments fall sharply.

The classroom no longer has to be in Vancouver

Online education changes the equation. A student in Brazil, Colombia, Chile, Mexico, or South Korea does not need to be in Vancouver to prepare for IELTS or CELPIP. Specialised instruction can begin before a student decides whether travelling to Canada is necessary at all.

For Canadian schools, this also changes the potential market they can reach. Instead of depending entirely on students physically arriving in Canada, small Vancouver-based online schools such as The LanguageSpace and EnglishforCanada can build relationships with students while they are still in their home countries.

This does not mean that online education will replace the traditional international-school experience. For many students, living in Vancouver and using English every day remains an important part of their educational and personal goals.

But the distinction between “coming to Canada to learn English” and “learning English from a Canadian school” is becoming less clear.

Vancouver’s language sector is not disappearing

The closure of EC and ILAC should not be interpreted as the end of Vancouver’s international language sector. Languages Canada represents more than 160 accredited language programs across nine provinces, indicating that a substantial network of language education remains in place.

What is changing is the structure of the market. The period when growing international enrolment could support ever-larger organisations and campuses has been disrupted. Schools now have to reconsider their costs, their markets and, perhaps most importantly, what students actually need.

Students, meanwhile, need better questions than, “Which school should I attend?”

They should ask whether the program matches their objective, how the institution is regulated or accredited, what protections exist for tuition payments and whether they really need a traditional full-time campus program. For someone whose immediate goal is an English test score, a specialised online program may be a practical alternative.

For Vancouver, the challenge is to preserve its reputation as an international education destination while adapting to a market that is smaller, more regulated, and increasingly digital.

The story of ILAC and EC may be more than a story about two companies that closed. It may mark the beginning of a new chapter in English language education where specialisation, personalisation, and adaptability matter as much as size.

title: US associations sue over ICE changes to international student internships
summary:
Four major US higher education associations have launched a legal challenge against the federal government over changes to rules governing internships and practical learning for international students.

The post US associations sue over ICE changes to international student internships appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The Association of American Universities (AAU), Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA and the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM) filed the lawsuit on October 5 against US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice.

At the centre of the dispute is Curricular Practical Training (CPT), which allows international students to undertake internships and other work-based learning connected to their academic programs,

The associations say ICE abruptly changed its interpretation of CPT requirements through two messages sent to universities in August, departing from a framework that institutions have relied on for more than 35 years.

Under the new interpretation, according to the complaint, international students would only qualify for CPT where the practical experience is mandatory for all students on a program. That could prevent international students from taking academically supervised internships or placements where they are elective rather than required for graduation.

The groups say the change has already prompted some institutions to pause or halt CPT authorisations, with some students losing internships secured months earlier.

We are going to court to protect our students and institutions

Miriam Feldblum, Presidents’ Alliance

“We are going to court to protect our students and institutions,” said Presidents’ Alliance president and CEO Miriam Feldblum, adding that the organisations are seeking to restore the longstanding CPT framework.

The lawsuit, filed in the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts, argues that the government introduced the change without formal rulemaking, public consultation or sufficient explanation.

The plaintiffs are seeking to prevent retroactive penalties and allow international students to continue accessing academically relevant practical training.

The lawsuit comes amid mounting uncertainty over international students’ access to work opportunities in the US, just days after the Trump administration proposed charging universities $70,000 for every international student they recommend for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

Under the proposal, institutions would also face a $30,000 annual fee for extensions of a student’s initial OPT period.

title: Trump targets $70m in international education funding as opposition grows
summary:
University groups are urging Congress to reverse the cuts, while seven states have challenged the administration’s wider effort to withhold funding approved by lawmakers.

The post Trump targets $70m in international education funding as opposition grows appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The Trump administration’s move to withdraw nearly USD $70 million from international education and foreign language programs has drawn opposition from university associations and lawmakers, as a broader legal challenge contests its authority to withhold the funding.

The money forms part of an $810 million package submitted to Congress on September 25, five days before the US fiscal year ended. The administration used a disputed mechanism known as a “pocket rescission” to withhold funding as its expiry date approached.

Since the announcement, six higher education associations have called for congressional intervention, while California and six other states have filed a lawsuit challenging the withholding of federal funds, including the latest package.

The formal White House request identifies $69.6 million for withdrawal from the Department of Education’s International Education and Foreign Language domestic programs. A separate provision targets $24.9 million from competitive grants for migrant students.

In its accompanying fact sheet, the White House labelled the international education funding “woke” and described the programs as supporting institutions bringing overseas students and faculty to the US for language teaching, research and professional development.

“These programs have deviated from their core mission and instead support wasteful and divisive projects, including doctoral dissertations on queer and trans community building in foreign countries,” it said.

This pocket rescission will result in significant harm to programs of national importance and goes directly against the congressional intent expressed in appropriations

Ted Mitchell, American Council on Education

American Council on Education president Ted Mitchell challenged that characterisation in a September 30 letter to congressional leaders, written on behalf of six higher education associations.

“Contrary to the administration’s justification for the rescission request, these programs serve a critical role in ensuring that America has sufficient expertise in areas vital to our national security and ability to compete globally,” Mitchell wrote.

The organisations backing the letter included the Association of American Universities and the Association of Public and Land-grant Universities. They urged Congress to reverse the rescission and prevent similar funding actions in future.

Mitchell said efforts to terminate or redirect appropriated funding had caused confusion for students, researchers and institutions, including applicants who had already competed for support.

The letter noted that the move followed changes to program names, an interagency agreement with the State Department and grant competitions held in June.

“This pocket rescission will result in significant harm to programs of national importance and goes directly against the congressional intent expressed in appropriations,” Mitchell wrote.

At the centre of the confrontation is whether a president can use the timing of a cancellation request to prevent congressionally approved money from being committed.

The Impoundment Control Act provides a 45-day period of continuous congressional session for lawmakers to consider a rescission request, during which funding may temporarily be withheld. A pocket rescission seeks to keep the money unavailable until it expires, effectively achieving a cancellation without congressional approval.

The White House argues that the law gives Trump authority to take this approach, describing it as a tool to eliminate spending that does not benefit American citizens.

However, the Government Accountability Office, Congress’s independent watchdog, concluded on September 29 that the administration could not withhold the funds through their expiry. It stressed that its opinion concerned compliance with spending law, rather than the merits of the programs targeted.

Republican senator Susan Collins, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, accused the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) of undermining Congress’s constitutional control over spending.

“OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding,” she said.

In their September 30 lawsuit, California and six other states — Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Nevada, New Mexico and Oregon — argue that withholding the funding violates the Constitution and the Administrative Procedure Act.

The PIE has contacted the White House, the OMB and the Department of Education for comment and is awaiting responses.

“Any effort to rescind appropriated funds without congressional approval is a clear violation of the law,” said Collins. “I will work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions.”

title: Moving Beyond the ‘Presentation Parade’: Designing Onboarding That Actually Teaches
summary:
​​​What words would you use to describe your back-to-school educator gathering? Kick off? Launch? Retreat? Presentation Parade? All too often, we educators forget to model what we know about how learning works when we gather for back-to-school work.   In my work helping to onboard ~125 Undergraduate Learning Assistants (ULAs) each August, our gathering has evolved […]

The post Moving Beyond the ‘Presentation Parade’: Designing Onboarding That Actually Teaches appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
What words would you use to describe your back-to-school educator gathering? Kick off? Launch? Retreat? Presentation Parade?

All too often, we educators forget to model what we know about how learning works when we gather for back-to-school work.

In my work helping to onboard ~125 Undergraduate Learning Assistants (ULAs) each August, our gathering has evolved over the last few years from a 3-hour “presentation parade” to interactive sessions modeling (and reflecting on) practices we want the ULAs to exemplify in their work and equipping them with the institutional information, skills, and context to be successful beginning their work.

Here’s how we made the change:

Backwards Design

What do you really want folks to take away from your gathering? What are your reasons to gather and how would you know if they had been met? We apply these backwards design principles in our teaching, and they are equally applicable – though often absent – for our meetings with educators.

If your gathering is primarily to disseminate information, it’s unlikely you need to gather. Consider instead sending a well-written and formatted email or a short video with the information you need to share.

If you want folks to use or do something with the information you want to share, shift the focus of the session to an activity that helps them build both the knowledge and the skill to do that something.

From Policies to Practice

The ULAs I work with need to be aware of several campus offices (Care Team, Ombuds, etc.) as well as University policies that apply to them as employees involved in education (FERPA, RVSM, etc.). Historically, we invited folks from each office or unit responsible to uphold the policy to come briefly explain their piece. Most presenters paused for questions, but it was primarily one-way communication, from the presenter to the room full of ULAs trapped in this presentation parade.

What I really need is for the ULAs to recognize that they are in a situation where one of those policies or campus office is relevant, and to know how to respond accordingly and/or ask for help. In collaboration with folks in the MSU Department of Mathematics, we developed a case study based, small group activity. Each group was assigned to find information about one campus unit or policy (links were provided) and discuss how to respond to a case study situation relevant to that office. We had one group for each unit or policy share out what they learned and how they would handle the case study scenario. These scenarios often elicited insightful, nuanced questions from other students and thus opportunities for deeper conversations about their work – the responsibilities, challenges, and opportunities. A brief but summative handout was provided at the end of the activity so that folks had a take-home resource that they could refer to later.

By more clearly articulating the goals of the session and better aligning the session activities, I shifted us from a passive parade to focused, small group work. This change gave the young educators the opportunity to build new knowledge, share their learnings with others who need that information, and awareness of realistic scenarios in which their new knowledge will be relevant.

Model the Work

Most educators have sat through a painfully ironic lecture about active learning.

Instead of propagating that experience, consider what approaches you might want to model for your educators – new and with various levels and types of prior experiences.

To help facilitate the small group activity described above, we hired and trained “ULAs to the ULAs” to support effective small group work in a large learning environment. These senior ULAs modeled the practices that we hope the ULAs enact in their work: moving between groups to start conversations, checking for understanding, encouraging participation from multiple folks, supporting the lead instructors’ sense of the progress and vibe of the room, and answering questions.

Most of the ULAs have been students in a course supported by a ULA, but that doesn’t mean that they were paying attention to what the ULA was doing during those class meetings. By modeling these teacher moves during the onboarding and taking a moment for folks to reflect on the work that the ULA trainers were doing, we helped model and surface in real time the kinds of inclusive, active strategies we hire the ULAs to incorporate across the 17+ courses that they support.

Honor Your Educators

Do you expect your educators to be human-centered, flexible, inclusive educators? If so, then you need to exemplify that in your back-to-school gathering.

What information about scope, timing, logistics, flexibility, and expectations would most help your educators physically, mentally, and relationally be present?

Provide the full agenda – including those new, clear goals – with timing cues ahead of the gathering. A week ahead would be best but aim for 2-3 business days minimum.

Provide information about where you are meeting: how to enter the building, where the room is in the building, where the bathrooms are near your meeting room, if there are outlets and power strips available in the meeting room, etc.

Intentionally plan (and staff) for flexible modalities, either async or hybrid.

If applicable, provide information about what sorts of beverages and food will be available, how allergies and food sensitivities will be accommodated.

Plan shorter sessions (1 hr max) with breaks between sessions.

While not exhaustive, the above list exemplifies some ways that leaders can show care for their educator community via planning and proactive clarity.

Conclusion

When we stopped thinking of onboarding as a place to deliver information and started treating it as a place to model learning, everything changed.

Our ULAs left not just with handouts, but with habits.

And that’s the invitation for all of us: to design our gatherings so that they look like the learning we hope to see.

For Reflection

How could you more carefully align the activities of your gathering with your actual reasons to gather? What part of your typical back-to-school gathering might be performative and thus not actually necessary?

What sorts of actions and strategies do you hope your educator community enacts in their classrooms? How could you model that in your back-to-school gathering?

What sorts of information and planning would exemplify the kind of care and inclusive, community-centered practices that are essential to your community?

Dr. Rachel Barnard is a teaching-focused faculty at Michigan State University, where she works with Undergraduate Learning Assistants (ULAs) across undergraduate STEM courses. Her work centers on educator development, inclusive teaching practices, and designing learning environments that help students and educators thrive. She is particularly interested in how institutions can better support early-career educators through intentional onboarding, reflective practice, and community-centered program design.

title: 2027 EDUCAUSE Top 10 Spotlights an Age of Change
summary:
Each year, the EDUCAUSE Top 10 report outlines the major trends, opportunities and challenges facing higher ed technology leaders, highlighting lessons learned from the year prior and forecasting what’s to come in the next year.
The 2027 EDUCAUSE Top 10 theme is the Age of Perpetual Change, spotlighting the pace of technological innovation in higher education and institutions’ abilities to adapt to it. The list was unveiled at the 2026 EDUCAUSE Annual Conference in Denver.
According to Mark McCormack, interim vice president of research, insights and analytics for EDUCAUSE, the theme of change…
full_text:
Artificial Intelligence Tops the 2027 EDUCAUSE Top 10 List

The collection of IT issues on the 2027 list highlights the ways higher education is adjusting to the change it’s currently being confronted with.

“There is all of this change happening, but we are seeing examples of institutions that are facing that head-on and are tackling the challenge of adapting,” McCormack says. “But they're not just adapting — they're adapting with purpose.”

The 2027 EDUCAUSE Top 10 list is:

Determining where AI adds real value

Future-proofing students for a volatile world

Balancing cybersecurity boundaries with autonomy and trust

Designing AI structures for responsible innovation

Designing human-centric technology experiences

Working creatively within real-world constraints

Building a strong and adaptive data governance backbone

Measuring and navigating enrollment shifts

Meeting stakeholders where they are with AI

Reducing friction for more seamless technology experiences

Artificial intelligence is mentioned on the list three times and takes the No. 1 spot. McCormack says this isn’t surprising, but the measured approach the contributors have taken to AI on the list is notable.

“You can see that we're all still in that messy space of trying to figure out what to do with AI and how to get a handle on it,” he says. “If you open up your social media feed, it can feel like an all-or-nothing debate right now. You're either a luddite who's tilting against windmills and you're going to get left behind, or you're a part of ushering in the end of the world — whatever kind of shape that debate takes on.”

INSIGHTS: Organizations are strategically approaching AI adoption.

McCormack warns that “ubiquity doesn’t equal utility,” meaning that just because AI is the buzzword of the moment, it doesn’t mean it’s right for every situation. It’s important for higher ed technology leaders to understand that distinction.

“I think it really is a great space for higher ed to walk into and model a more nuanced, critical approach to this moment,” he says. “AI is a tool that, like any other tool, can be useful, but let's be thoughtful and honest about where it can actually add value, where it can do harm and pose risks, and where it fits with our culture and goals as an institution.”

Higher Ed IT Teams Are Seeking Balance

Another theme woven through this year’s list is balance. Regarding issue No. 3, for example, McCormack says institutions are balancing strength and structure with autonomy and flexibility in a cybersecurity context.

“We know that the individual user is one of the biggest areas of vulnerability for an institution,” he says. “To me, that's one of the clearest areas where we need to have a shared understanding of what our security posture is and how to protect and be sensitive to those things. But we also have to empower, train and equip the individual person to be that discerning, confident decision-maker in the moment when they don't have their CISO standing over their shoulder.”

LEARN MORE: Assessments can help shape higher ed security strategies.

The report notes that to achieve this while navigating the current security landscape, there must be an institutional culture of communication, mutual understanding and trust.

There is also balance to be found in weaving the human element into the technology experience, particularly in the AI era. With issue No. 5, IT leaders are focused on designing human-centered experiences.

“I think issue No. 5 is the clearest and boldest declaration of the value of designing our systems, tools and technology experiences with the human person in mind,” McCormack said, “with what they need — and even more specifically, with accessibility — in mind, designing our technology ecosystems in ways that are equitable and that don't put up barriers to important stakeholders and people in the community.”

This means everything from moving beyond checklists and meeting basic compliance mandates to conducting outreach for a deeper understanding the needs of each distinct, diverse campus community, the report says.

Click the banner below to subscribe to our weekly newsletter.

Addressing Challenges Requires Planning and Analysis

The EDUCAUSE Top 10 also addresses challenges in higher education, including resource constraints, enrollment trends and digital friction.

For issue No. 6, the report highlights institutions that are working creatively under resource and staffing constraints. The 2026 EDUCAUSE Workforce Report discusses a cycle of reactivity in which technology teams don’t have the resources to be proactive in their work and instead must work just to keep their heads above water. This issue addresses the resource-constrained cycle that higher ed IT teams are facing, McCormack says.

“It’s a persistent thing we've picked up from our members,” he says. “They're stressed, and a lot of them are burned out. They feel under-resourced, whether in terms of budget or the staff that they need to support their central services and the work that they need to do.”

So, how are technology teams responding to this cycle? The answer is no longer doing more with less, McCormack says. Instead, institutions are looking for ways to free up time using automation, AI and resource sharing both within and outside their institutions.

DISCOVER: Frictionless digital spaces improve the end user experience.

“I think there is an opportunity to take a step back and evaluate how are we working,” McCormack says. “Are we actually maximizing our resources? Are we working in the in the most efficient ways or are there opportunities that are right in front of us of things we can do differently to rethink how we operate as a team?”

Issue No. 8 notes that the enrollment cliff is no longer hypothetical; many institutions report that it’s already here. McCormack says the best way to understand enrollment shifts is to look at the data.

“This issue gets into how we are equipping our senior leaders and decision-makers with trustworthy and compelling data so they get the full picture of what's happening,” he says. “How can our institution move forward and navigate these demographic shifts?”

For issue No. 10, the list concludes with the need to reduce friction and remove barriers from technology access for a more seamless end-user experience. According to McCormack, today’s rapidly changing technology environment means institutions are acting quickly to implement new tools and technologies. This can lead to technology debt and cluttered IT ecosystems that are redundant or clunky to use.

UP NEXT: Continuous threat exposure management helps higher ed prioritize risk.

“One example of that would be as a student, I'm trying to complete a task for a course, and I've got multiple systems that I have to log in to separately to accomplish what I need to do,” McCormack says. “Institutions that are looking to address friction might take those different systems and integrate them into a single access point, so that the student can just get in and get what they need through that single point.”

Ultimately, McCormack says, institutions that are adapting well to the rapid changes facing higher education are no longer acting spontaneously when making technology decisions.

“They're staying anchored to what they value and what their goals and mission are as an institution, and they're adapting with people at the center of it,” he says. “It's encouraging to me that we're seeing adaptation happening thoughtfully.”

title: Internationales Benchmarking des thailändischen Hochschulsystems
summary: Wie leistungsfähig ist das thailändische Hochschulsystem, wo liegen seine besonderen Stärken und wie positionieren sich die Hochschulen im internationalen Vergleich? Im Auftrag...
full_text:
Wie leistungsfähig ist das thailändische Hochschulsystem, wo liegen seine besonderen Stärken und wie positionieren sich die Hochschulen im internationalen Vergleich? Im Auftrag des Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research, and Innovation (MHESI) in Thailand hat das CHE Centrum für Hochschulentwicklung ein umfassendes Benchmarking des thailändischen Hochschulsystems durchgeführt. Mit dem Abschlussbericht ist das Projekt nun abgeschlossen.

Ziel war es, eine fundierte Datengrundlage für die strategische Weiterentwicklung der Hochschulen in Thailand zu schaffen und zugleich Vergleiche mit europäischen Hochschulen zu ermöglichen. Methodische Grundlage war der Ansatz des European Higher Education Sector Observatory (EHESO), der auf den Erfahrungen von U-Multirank aufbaut. Anders als klassische Rankings betrachtet dieser Ansatz Hochschulen nicht anhand einer einzigen Rangliste, sondern differenziert nach mehreren Leistungsdimensionen.

69 Hochschulen und fast 20.000 Studierende

Für das Benchmarking wurden institutionelle Daten zu 69 thailändischen Hochschulen zusammengeführt. Sie stammen sowohl aus einer Befragung der Hochschulen als auch aus Daten des thailändischen Ministeriums. Analysiert wurden sieben Dimensionen: Research, Resources, Teaching & Learning, Knowledge Transfer, Regional Engagement, International Orientation und Societal Challenges.

Ergänzt wurde die institutionelle Perspektive durch eine umfangreiche Studierendenbefragung. 47 Hochschulen beteiligten sich daran. Nach der Datenbereinigung konnten die Angaben von 19.698 Studierenden ausgewertet werden. Die Befragung erfasste unter anderem die Qualität der Lehre, Studienorganisation, Praxiserfahrungen, Digitalisierung, Internationalisierung, Infrastruktur, Nachhaltigkeit und Diversität.

Unterschiedliche Hochschultypen – unterschiedliche Stärken

Die Ergebnisse zeigen vor allem, dass das thailändische Hochschulsystem stark differenziert ist. Die Hochschulen folgen keinem einheitlichen Leistungsprofil, sondern übernehmen unterschiedliche Funktionen innerhalb des Systems.

Forschungsuniversitäten (Frontier Research Universities) zeigen besondere Stärken in Forschung, Ressourcen und internationaler Orientierung. Technologie- und innovationsorientierte Universitäten (Technology and Innovation Universities) weisen ein stärker anwendungs- und innovationsorientiertes Profil auf. Regional verankerte Universitäten (Area-Based and Community Universities) spielen insbesondere für die regionale Versorgung und Entwicklung eine wichtige Rolle. Spezialisierte und berufsorientierte Universitäten (Specialized and Professional Universities) zeigen unter anderem Stärken in Studium und Lehre sowie im Wissenstransfer.

Auf Ebene des gesamten Hochschulsystems gehören besonders regionale Verankerung sowie Studium und Lehre zu den Stärken. Im Vergleich zum Durchschnitt der mehr als 3.400 europäischen Hochschulen im EHESO-Datensatz zeigen thailändische Hochschulen eine vergleichsweise starke MINT-Orientierung und hohe Studierendenzahlen. Entwicklungsmöglichkeiten zeigen sich zugleich unter anderem bei der Internationalisierung, der externen Forschungsfinanzierung und beim unternehmerischen Wissenstransfer.

Studierende bewerten ihr Studium positiv

Auch aus Sicht der Studierenden ergibt sich insgesamt ein positives Bild. Nahezu alle untersuchten Bereiche erreichen im Durchschnitt Bewertungen von mindestens vier Punkten auf einer fünfstufigen Skala. Besonders positiv beurteilen die Studierenden die Diversität an ihren Hochschulen, die Organisation der Studienprogramme und den Kontakt zu Lehrenden. Gleichzeitig zeigen die Ergebnisse Unterschiede zwischen Fächern, Hochschultypen und Governance-Formen. Damit liefert die Studierendenbefragung eine wichtige zusätzliche Perspektive auf die institutionellen Daten und ermöglicht eine differenziertere Einordnung der Studienbedingungen.

Grundlage für weitere Hochschulentwicklung

Mit dem Projekt steht den beteiligten Hochschulen und dem thailändischen Ministerium eine umfassende Grundlage zur Verfügung, um institutionelle Profile sichtbar zu machen, Stärken zu identifizieren und Entwicklungsmöglichkeiten zu erkennen. Der internationale Vergleich hilft zudem dabei, die Besonderheiten des thailändischen Hochschulsystems im Verhältnis zu europäischen Hochschulen einzuordnen.

Der vollständige Abschlussbericht mit Methodik, Ergebnissen und detaillierten Analysen ist hier verfügbar:
